claims.claim: OpenStax's Principles of Management defines leadership as a social (interpersonal) influence relationship between two or more persons who depend on each other to attain certain mutual goals in a group situation.
Leading, as one of the classic management functions, is the people function: influencing and motivating people to work toward the organization's goals.
Managers are generally appointed to their role, whereas leadership per se is a relationship that revolves around the followers' acceptance or rejection of the leader.
A good leader develops a vision for the group, communicates that vision, and orchestrates the group's energy and activity toward goal attainment.

Managers commonly derive power from the organization and the position they occupy, while leaders more commonly derive influence from followers' perception of their expertise, personality, and the working relationship developed with followers.

Leadership is a process: a complex and dynamic exchange relationship built over time between leader and follower, in which the leader influences the followers and the followers influence the leader, within a context that shapes both.
Follower behavior plays a major role in determining what behaviors leaders engage in.
Developing people is part of leadership work; OpenStax describes transformational leaders' individualized consideration as a focus on the development of the follower.
The leading function of management includes leading and motivating people, communicating, resolving conflicts, and managing change (OpenStax Introduction to Business 6.1).
No one leadership style fits all organizations or situations; the right approach depends on the situation and the people.
A leader can be anyone in an organization, regardless of position, able to influence others to act or follow, often by their own choice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether management and leadership are the same thing
positions: Some everyday usage treats every manager as a leader by virtue of position and uses the two terms interchangeably.
OpenStax distinguishes them: managers are generally appointed, while leadership revolves around followers' acceptance or rejection and can be exercised without any title.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the OpenStax distinction, notes that the two overlap in practice (the best managers also lead), and defers the full comparison to the sibling topic management-versus-leadership.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that 'Leading is a foundational concept in Management & Leadership' — generic boilerplate with no content.
The generated draft's claim that 'College courses use leading as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' — generic boilerplate, not supported by the research.
The generated draft's Eli-10 toolbox-drawer analogy ('Think of leading as a label on a toolbox drawer') — generic boilerplate using banned phrasing; replaced with an original hiking analogy.
